'''Charles Thorn''' (born 14 August 1946) is an American physicist who is a Professor of [[Physics]] at [[University of Florida]] in [[Gainesville, Florida]].<ref>[http://www.phys.ufl.edu/faculty/thorn.shtml Charles Thorn at University of Florida]</ref> He played an important role in the development of dual models and [[string theory]].<ref>Goddard P. From dual models to string theory, ''The Birth of String Theory'' (18–19 May 2007)] {{Arxiv|0802.3249v1}} (accessed 16 April 2008)</ref> Among his contributions is the proof of the non-existence of [[Ghost (physics)|ghosts]] in string theory. The [[Goddard–Thorn theorem]] is a result about certain [[vector space]]s in [[string theory]]. Thorn developed it with [[Peter Goddard (physicist)|Peter Goddard]].

==Education and personal life==
Thorn obtained his undergraduate degree in [[physics]] at [[Massachusetts Institute of Technology]] (MIT) and completed his Ph.D. in [[physics]] from [[University of California, Berkeley]] in 1971 under the supervision of [[Stanley Mandelstam]]. He has held postdoctoral positions at MIT and [[CERN]].<ref>{{Cite book|last1=Cappelli|first1=Andrea|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=WNZyoUteXIkC&q=%22Charles+Thorn%22+cern&pg=PA246|title=The Birth of String Theory|last2=Castellani|first2=Elena|last3=Colomo|first3=Filippo|last4=Vecchia|first4=Paolo Di|date=2012-04-12|publisher=Cambridge University Press|isbn=978-0-521-19790-8|language=en}}</ref> He is fond of [[tango]] dancing.{{cn|date=August 2020}}

==Research==
Charles Thorn also has developed an approach to string theory based on the idea of string bits.<ref>Strings Branes and Gravity. [[Jeffrey A. Harvey]], [[Shamit Kachru]], [[Eva Silverstein]]. World Scientific TASI 1999</ref><ref>Reformulating String Theory with the [[1/N expansion]]. {{arXiv|hep-th/9405069}}</ref> This idea led him to the conclusion that in this formalism one of the dimensions of spacetime appears to be dynamic. The fundamental degrees of freedom propagated on a surface in one lower dimension thus giving a [[holographic principle|holographic theory]].

He was elected a [[Fellow of the American Physical Society]] in 1989 ''"For important contributions to the theory of elementary particles. Nominated by: Division of Particles and Fields"''.<ref> {{cite web|url=https://www.aps.org/programs/honors/fellowships/archive-all.cfm?initial=&year=1989&unit_id=&institution=|title=APS Fellow Archive|publisher=APS|access-date= 5 October 2020}} </ref>
